Bonds and Debentures: Types, Pricing, Yield and Credit Ratings

A bond is a loan you give to a government or a company, in return for interest and repayment on a set date. This guide covers the types, how to price a bond, and why prices fall when interest rates rise.

2 min readFor MBA, BBA and BBMUpdated 2 November 2026

The features of a bond

FeatureMeaningExample
Face valueThe amount repaid at maturity₹1,000
Coupon rateYearly interest on face value8%, or ₹80 a year
MaturityThe repayment date5 years
IssuerThe borrowerGovernment of India, or a company
Credit ratingAn opinion on safetyAAA to D

Types of bonds

  • Government securities (G-Secs) and T-bills: issued by the government, with very low default risk.
  • State development loans: issued by state governments.
  • Corporate bonds and debentures: issued by companies, with higher yields and credit risk.
  • Zero-coupon bonds: pay no coupon, and are issued at a discount to face value.
  • Convertible bonds: can be turned into shares.
  • Floating-rate bonds: the coupon moves with a benchmark.
  • Tax-free and capital gains bonds: with special tax treatment, under specific rules.
  • Green bonds: for environmental projects.
  • Junk bonds: rated below investment grade, with a high yield and high risk.

Bonds and debentures compared

The two words are often used interchangeably. In Indian usage, a debenture usually means a company's debt, which may be secured or unsecured, while a bond is often issued by a government or public body and is usually secured or government-backed. Debenture holders are creditors, not owners, and have no voting rights.

How a bond is priced

A bond's price is the present value of its coupons and face value, discounted at the market's required yield.

Face value ₹1,000, coupon 8% (₹80 a year), 5 years, market yield 10%. Price = 80 × 3.7908 + 1,000 × 0.6209 = 303.26 + 620.92 = ₹924.18.

This bond trades at a discount because its 8% coupon is below the 10% the market wants. If the market yield were 8%, the bond would trade at par (₹1,000). If it were lower than 8%, the bond would trade at a premium.

Yield measures

MeasureFormulaResult
Coupon yieldCoupon ÷ face value80 ÷ 1,000 = 8%
Current yieldCoupon ÷ market price80 ÷ 924.18 = 8.66%
Approximate YTM[C + (F − P) ÷ n] ÷ [(F + P) ÷ 2]95.16 ÷ 962.09 = 9.89%
Exact YTMThe rate that sets PV equal to the price10%

Why prices fall when rates rise

If new bonds pay 10%, nobody will pay full price for your 8% bond, so its price has to fall until its yield matches. This is interest rate risk. Duration measures it: a bond with a duration of 5 years falls about 5% for a 1 percentage point rise in yields. Longer-dated and lower-coupon bonds are more sensitive.

The risks

  • Interest rate risk: prices fall when rates rise.
  • Credit risk: the issuer may not pay. Ratings from CRISIL, ICRA and CARE help, but they aren't guarantees.
  • Reinvestment risk: coupons may have to be reinvested at lower rates.
  • Inflation risk: fixed coupons buy less over time.
  • Liquidity risk: many Indian corporate bonds trade thinly.

Exam and interview questions

Why do bond prices and yields move in opposite directions?

A bond's cash flows are fixed. To offer a higher yield to a new buyer, its price must fall, and to offer a lower yield, its price must rise.

What is a zero-coupon bond?

A bond that pays no interest, sold at a discount and repaid at face value. The difference is the investor's return.

What is the difference between current yield and YTM?

Current yield looks only at this year's coupon relative to price. YTM also includes the gain or loss to maturity and the time value of money.

How can a retail investor buy government bonds in India?

Through the RBI Retail Direct platform, through a broker on the exchange, or indirectly through gilt funds.
